strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: severe class imbalance in semi-supervised node classification. Retrieving existing unlabeled nodes avoids synthesizing features and edges and remains applicable when a minority class has only one labeled example.

The reported evaluation is broad, covering five datasets, three GNN architectures, imbalance ratios up to 100, and naturally imbalanced settings. Several gains are substantial: on Cora with GCN at ratio 10, F1 improves from the strongest listed baseline’s 72.14 to 76.44.

Pseudo-label accuracy diagnostics, component ablations, and sensitivity experiments provide useful empirical investigation beyond aggregate benchmark scores. The appendix documents training procedures, hyperparameter ranges, and hardware. No material ethical concern is evident from the manuscript.
weaknesses: The advance over the closest prior work is insufficiently established. The cited M3S already uses clustering assignments to filter classifier-generated pseudo-labels, closely overlapping DPAM. The DPAM-plus-confidence ablation partially addresses this comparison, but a directly matched M3S evaluation across the main settings is missing. Consequently, improvements over synthetic oversampling methods do not establish the same degree of progress over existing graph self-training.

Supporting statistics contain internal inconsistencies that require correction. In Table 8, GCN at ratio 5 reports 11,593.6 aligned and 2,308.4 discarded nodes, totaling 13,902 rather than the stated 13,632 unlabeled nodes. Table 9 reports 96.40 ± 4.27 as an accuracy with standard error over five repetitions; with this mean and accuracies bounded by 100%, the usual sample standard error cannot exceed 3.60 percentage points. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the diagnostic evidence and uncertainty reporting.

The evidence for the additional mechanisms is mixed. Table 11 shows almost identical PubMed F1 for geometric ranking alone and the complete method, while adding DGIN to node reordering reduces the CiteSeer mean. There is no comparison against a simple fixed-weight ranking combination to establish the value of RBO-based weighting. The proposed geometric imbalance measure also closely resembles ordinary nearest-centroid ambiguity; its distinct significance for class imbalance is not convincingly isolated.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Equation 7 combines ordered lists without explicitly defining the per-node numerical ranks being combined. Section 4.3 treats the assigned class center as the nearest center to each node, although cluster-level assignment in Equation 4 does not guarantee this. Algorithm 1 does not explicitly apply the per-class addition limit or update the unlabeled pool. The manuscript provides no code link, selected configurations, or F1 averaging convention to resolve these ambiguities.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 2 shows UNREAL underperforming GraphENS+TAM on both GraphSAGE metrics, contradicting the stated consistent superiority on naturally imbalanced datasets. Computational advantages are also insufficiently quantified: the method permits 40–100 training rounds with up to 2,000 epochs per round, but reports no end-to-end runtime or peak-memory comparison. The substantial reported gains are promising, but the closest-baseline gap and verification problems outweigh them in the current submission.
